claims.text: Sintering the Mg-Al-Ti-V-Fe-Co alloy at 900–980 °C causes transient precipitation of a continuous nanocrystalline (Al,Ti)-rich B2 network at grain boundaries.
The B2 network suppresses Mg volatilization.
The B2 network retards inward oxygen diffusion.
The diffusion barrier enables formation of a dense protective passive film rich in Al2O3 and TiO2.
The ball-milled starting powder is a metastable BCC solid solution.
The ball-milled powder has a nanocrystalline grain size below 50 nm.
The starting powder has high lattice strain.
Significant oxygen is trapped at grain boundaries in the starting powder.
The proposed SPS window is 900–980 °C for 5–15 minutes under 50–80 MPa in vacuum or ultra-pure argon, followed by rapid cooling.
Diffusion at 900–980 °C drives Al and Ti segregation to grain boundaries and nucleation of the B2 phase.
The proposed B2 phase has significantly lower Mg and O diffusion coefficients than the BCC matrix.
The precipitate network changes oxidation from a surface-reaction-controlled MgO-forming regime to a diffusion-controlled Al2O3/TiO2-scale-forming regime.
Material sintered within the proposed window will exceed 98% theoretical density.
Material sintered within the proposed window will have more than 30% greater Vickers hardness than material sintered below 800 °C.
The parabolic oxidation rate constant will be one order of magnitude lower than for samples sintered at 800 °C or 1000 °C.
Sintering below 800 °C produces porous, low-hardness material because diffusion is insufficient for densification and phase separation.
Sintering at 1000 °C causes severe Mg loss, porosity, compositional inhomogeneity, and poor oxidation resistance.
The proposed mechanism fails above 990 °C or after holding longer than 20 minutes because Mg volatilization overcomes the precipitate barrier.
Exceeding the temperature or time boundary dissolves the B2 network and produces a porous, Mg-depleted matrix.
Linear oxidation kinetics indicate surface-reaction control, whereas parabolic kinetics indicate diffusion control by a protective barrier.
